definition: Meant to calm someone's anger or end a disagreement by making peace.
example: After the tense meeting, the manager sent a conciliatory email offering to share credit for the project.
nuance: Conciliatory gestures aim to restore goodwill, while appeasing often suggests giving in too much just to avoid conflict.
prompt: Two neighbors have been arguing for months over a fence on their shared property line.
options: Hoping to end the feud, Mr. Ortiz made a conciliatory offer to split the cost of a new fence.
Ms. Lane sent a conciliatory note demanding the fence come down by Friday or she would call a lawyer.
His conciliatory reply was only four words long, so the other neighbor read it in a second.
When the survey proved him right, the conciliatory neighbor gloated loudly over the fence for an hour.
reasons: Offering to share the expense is a peace-making move meant to ease the conflict.
An ultimatum with a threat escalates the dispute instead of soothing it.
This confuses the word with concise; shortness says nothing about making peace.
Gloating rubs in a victory and would inflame the other neighbor, not calm them.

practice.prompt: A team captain snapped at a teammate during practice and now wants to repair the relationship.
options: The next morning, the captain struck a conciliatory tone and admitted she had been too harsh.
In a conciliatory speech to the whole team, the captain blamed the teammate for every missed pass.
The captain gave a conciliatory cheer when the same teammate scored the winning goal later that week.
To show she was conciliatory, the captain refused to speak to the teammate for the rest of the week.
reasons: Admitting fault in a gentle way is an effort to smooth things over.
Publicly blaming someone deepens the hurt rather than mending it.
This mixes the word up with congratulatory; cheering a goal is praise, not peacemaking.
The silent treatment keeps the conflict going instead of resolving it.
